title: Connection Pooling & Sizing
description: Optimize PostgreSQL connection pools, size max_connections, configure PgBouncer in transaction mode, and prevent thrashing.

data.text: A counter-intuitive fact of database engineering is that **fewer connections yield higher throughput**. When hundreds of backend processes compete for CPU caches and disk I/O, context-switching thrashing degrades performance.

A proven formula for PostgreSQL pool sizing is: `connections = ((CPU_cores * 2) + effective_spindle_count)`. For an 8-core server on SSD storage, an active pool of ~16 to 25 connections will achieve peak throughput!

PgBouncer keeps a small pool of real server connections and multiplexes many client connections onto them. In `transaction` pooling mode, a server connection is returned to the pool at the end of each transaction, which gives the best multiplexing. The catch is that session-scoped state — prepared statements, `SET` values, advisory locks, and session-level `LISTEN` — does not survive between transactions.

data.title: A minimal PgBouncer configuration
data.content: The pool size stays close to the connection formula while hundreds of application connections share it.
data.code:
[databases]
app = host=127.0.0.1 port=5432 dbname=app

[pgbouncer]
listen_addr = 0.0.0.0
listen_port = 6432
auth_type = scram-sha-256
auth_file = /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt

pool_mode = transaction
max_client_conn = 1000
default_pool_size = 20
reserve_pool_size = 5
server_idle_timeout = 60

# Required if the app uses named prepared statements
max_prepared_statements = 100

data.title: Transaction pooling breaks session state
data.text: Because a client may land on a different server connection for each transaction, anything that lives for the session can be lost: `SET` commands, temporary tables, advisory locks, cursors outside a transaction, and session-level prepared statements. If your driver caches named prepared statements, enable `max_prepared_statements` on PgBouncer or use statement mode. Assuming session state is preserved is the most common PgBouncer bug.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use PgBouncer in transaction mode in front of PostgreSQL for serverless or microservice architectures.
Higher connection counts cause CPU context-switching thrash.
